passages.title: A Speech That Divided the Room
passages.text:
Last week a young **politician** visited our university to give a talk. Her advice was **sensible**: save money, listen carefully and never promise more than you can deliver. A few students laughed and said that voting was a **silly** idea, but she answered them calmly and without anger.

Then she spoke about her grandmother, who raised three children alone. It was an **emotional** moment, and the hall went completely quiet. The speaker **became emotional** herself, and several students wiped their eyes.

Afterwards I felt **confused**. I had come to the hall expecting to disagree with her, yet I found myself clapping loudly. The whole experience was **confusing** because my head and my heart were saying different things. I told myself not to **confuse** a good speaker with a good plan, and I decided to read her proposals carefully before making up my mind.

passages.title: Curiosity and Green Eyes
passages.text:
My little sister Lan has always been a **curious** child. She asks why the sky is blue, how fish breathe and where the wind goes at night. Her **curiosity** sometimes gets her into trouble, like the day she took apart our father's radio. When she opened it, she looked at the wires **curiously**, then smiled.

Lan is usually **cheerful**, humming songs all morning. Last month, however, she became **miserable**. Her best friend had started playing with another girl, and Lan was **jealous** of her. She watched them **jealously** from the garden fence and refused to eat dinner.

Our mother sat beside her and explained that **jealousy** is a normal feeling, but it can hurt friendships if we let it grow. She suggested that Lan invite both girls to our house. The next weekend the three of them were laughing together, and my sister was her **cheerful** self again.

passages.title: When Sleep and Mood Go Wrong
passages.text:
According to a recent health report, millions of people **suffer from** a **mental disorder** at some point in their lives. The word **disorder** describes a condition that disturbs normal thinking, feeling or behaviour. It is not a sign of weakness.

Some of the most common problems are **sleep disorders**, such as insomnia, which leave people tired and unable to concentrate. Others experience **anxiety disorders**, where constant worry takes over daily life. Teenagers may also develop **eating disorders**, in which food becomes a source of fear or control.

Stress at work can **depress** even strong, confident people. A manager who loses a project may feel **depressed** for weeks and stop seeing friends. Doctors say that early help makes a big difference, so anyone with long-lasting symptoms should talk to a professional rather than wait.

passages.title: Pounds, Notes and a Quiet Argument
passages.text:
Studying in London was exciting but sometimes **depressing**. The grey weather lasted for weeks, and Hoa began to worry that she might slip into **depression**. A friend advised her to go out and move her body, so she started to run **energetically** along the river every morning, and her mood improved quickly.

Money was another worry. The British **currency** is called **sterling**, and Hoa had to learn the value of every **note** in her purse. At first she **was frightened of** using the wrong one in shops, and she even **was frightened of** asking for help.

Things became more serious when her landlord claimed she owed extra fees. Hoa believed this was wrong, and the **dispute** lasted a month. In the end the student union helped her to show the receipts, and the landlord apologised. She finally felt that life in the city was more welcoming than she had feared.

passages.title: Paying for University
passages.text:
When Minh arrived at university, his pockets were full of **coin**s and his head was full of questions about money. His parents could not pay everything, so he decided to **get a loan** from the government. A **student loan** has a low interest rate, and you only start repaying it when you have a good job.

He had to **pay his fees** in September, and he felt relieved when the money arrived in his bank account. After that, he checked the balance regularly. As long as he **was in credit**, he felt safe.

When he needed cash, he walked to the nearest **cashpoint**, a machine on the corner of the campus. His American roommate calls it **a cash machine**, but both words mean the same thing. Minh usually chose to **take out money** on Friday only, which stopped him from spending too much during the week. By following this simple habit, he finished his first term without any financial stress.

passages.title: Renting a First Flat
passages.text:
Nga wanted her own flat, but she soon learned how expensive it could be. She **owed her brother money** because he had lent her some for the first month. She promised to **pay back** the **amount of money** within a year.

Her salary was small, so she decided to **save up for** a laptop instead of buying one immediately. A new phone was also something she **couldn't afford**, so she kept her old one.

Every month she had to **pay rent** on the first day. The landlord asked for **one month's rent** as a safety fee, and she also had to **pay a deposit** before she got the keys. The deposit would be returned when she left the flat clean and undamaged.

Nga kept a notebook with every expense. It helped her understand where her money went, and slowly she began to feel in control of her life.

passages.text:
Last Saturday I went shopping with my cousin. She wanted to **borrow** a camera **from** me, but I decided to **lend** her **my old one** instead. In return, she promised that she would help me find a good coat.

It was **likely** that the shops would be crowded, and we **were likely to** wait in long queues. At the first store, all scarves **were on special offer**, and the sign said **three for the price of two**. I bought three, and my cousin laughed because I do not even wear scarves.

Later I realised one of them had a hole, so I returned to the shop. The assistant was polite and quickly gave me a **refund**. At the market, we managed to **agree a lower price** on a bag after a short talk with the seller. By evening we had spent less than we planned, and we were both delighted.

passages.text:
On Sunday mornings a small market opens beside the park, and I love to **haggle** there. The first rule is to be friendly. If you **haggle over the price** with a smile, the seller often gives you a better deal. Once I bought a pair of boots, and when they did not fit, I easily **took** them **back** to the stall.

The market is reached by a quiet **footpath** that follows the river. In autumn the path is covered by **leaves**, and every **branch** above is bright orange. Some trees have enormous **roots** that push through the soil and break the stones.

My grandfather, a retired banker, once told me about a **certificate of deposit**, a safe way to save money for several years. I laughed because I only had enough for a bag of apples, but I found his advice interesting. We walked home slowly, talking and eating fruit.

passages.text:
Last Monday there was a **tense meeting** at our office. My manager **raised his voice at** a new colleague and complained that a report was late. Writing reports was not even in her **job description**, but he shouted at her **in front of people** anyway. The whole room went silent, and several of us looked at the floor.

After the meeting, he said he had spoken like that **in the heat of the moment**. I do not accept this as an excuse. A good manager should **address** a colleague **about** a problem calmly, in a private **one-on-one** talk, not in public.

To his credit, he later met her alone and told her that this was the **absolute last time** he would lose his temper. She listened quietly and asked for a written copy of her duties. I believe the incident taught everyone in the department an important lesson about respect.

passages.title: The Garden Argument
passages.text:
Our neighbour, Mr Brown, takes great pride in his garden. One afternoon my twelve-year-old son rode his bike too fast and had to **brake hard** to avoid hitting a dog. The bike slid across the **grass** and left deep marks in the **ground**. Worse still, it crushed a rare **plant** that Mr Brown had been growing for years.

He was furious, and I was afraid of a long fight. Instead, we decided to **have a conversation like adults**. I told my son he was **mature enough** to say sorry for himself, so he stepped forward and **apologized for his behavior**. He explained that he had been scared of the dog.

Mr Brown took a deep breath and nodded. He said the damage could be repaired, **as long as it doesn't happen again**. The next weekend my son helped him plant new flowers, and the two became unexpected friends.

passages.title: A Well-Equipped Classroom
passages.text:
Mrs Hang's English classroom is simple but very practical. Each desk holds a few useful tools. A **rubber** sits beside every pencil, so that students can **rub out** a mistake without making a mess. A wooden **ruler** lies next to it, and pupils **measure** the lines on their diagrams carefully.

In reading lessons, learners use a **highlighter pen** to mark key words in yellow. The teacher says that colours help memory. At the back of the room, a long cable ends in a **plug**, and the nearest **socket** is hidden behind the cupboard. Last week Mrs Hang needed to use a projector, and it took her five minutes to find it.

Pupils usually sit with a **partner** because they learn more when they share ideas. When one student makes an error, the other politely corrects it. This friendly system has made the class one of the most popular in the school.

passages.title: Classroom Habits
passages.text:
In our class, small actions make lessons smoother. When the teacher wants to **highlight** a rule, she writes it on the board in red. If she wants to show a video, someone must **plug** the laptop **in** and test the sound. Sometimes the music is too quiet, and we ask her to **turn** it **up**. When it is too loud, we ask her to **turn** it **down**.

Students often forget stationery, so they **borrow** a pen **from** a classmate. I usually **lend** my friend Tuan my pencil case, and he always gives it back. Last week I also had to **lend** my notebook **to** Linh, who was absent.

An important habit is to **correct each other's English** politely. Tuan once told me that I said 'informations', and I thanked him because it helps me improve. A friendly classroom, in my opinion, depends on mutual help.

passages.title: Asking Good Questions in English
passages.text:
In my English class, we often **work with a partner**. It is easier to practise speaking when there is someone to talk to, and we always **share** a book **with** each other. One student reads a sentence, and the other **repeats** it **after** the speaker.

When we meet a new word, we ask polite questions. **What does** 'reluctant' **mean**? **How do you pronounce** 'laughter'? **How do you spell** 'necessary'? **How do you use the word** 'although' in a sentence? These questions are simple, but they save a lot of time and prevent embarrassing mistakes.

Sometimes two words look similar, and we need help. Our teacher can **explain the difference between** 'lend' **and** 'borrow', and she gives real examples from life. After a few weeks of this routine, I noticed my vocabulary growing quickly and my confidence rising.

passages.title: Schools Then and Now
passages.text:
**In the past**, school was very strict. Pupils sat in silent rows and had to **write an essay** every Friday on a topic chosen by the teacher. If someone made a mistake, the teacher might **call** them **a lazy student** in front of everyone. Boys and girls wore the same uniform and could not **dress** the way they wanted.

**Nowadays**, many schools have a friendly **atmosphere**. Classrooms are **relaxed**, and students are encouraged to talk and discuss ideas. Lessons about English sounds may include a clear **consonant** chart, such as p, b, t and d, because pronunciation is taught seriously.

Some parents miss the old discipline, but most agree that children learn better when they feel comfortable. A good school, in the end, is not one where students are afraid, but one where they enjoy discovering new things and are free to ask questions.

passages.title: Speaking Up Without Fear
passages.text:
When Linh started learning English, she found the **vowel** sounds especially difficult. Short and long vowels, such as the ones in 'ship' and 'sheep', seemed identical to her. Even so, she was **willing to** practise every day, and she recorded herself on her phone. Her main goal was to **make herself understood** when she travelled abroad.

She also liked to **experiment with** new words, trying them in different sentences until they felt natural. Her teacher encouraged this approach and often said that mistakes are a normal step.

After six months, Linh decided to **take an exam** to measure her progress. Her friend Hung had to **do an exam** at the same centre, so they went together. Linh was nervous but managed to **pass the exam**, while Hung unfortunately **failed the exam** because he had skipped practice. Both agreed that the experience had been useful and that the next attempt would go better.

passages.title: Second Chances in Exams
passages.text:
Tuan was disappointed when he first **did badly** in his maths test. He had **revised for** only one day, and he panicked halfway through. Instead of giving up, he decided to **retake the exam** the following term.

This time he made a plan. He studied every evening and asked his teacher for help. On the day, he told himself to **do his best** and not to worry about the result. His sister gave him the same advice and told him to **try his best**, which calmed him.

When the results arrived, Tuan found that he could **do well** after all. He was proud to **get a good grade** in algebra, and his class teacher also wrote that he had earned a surprisingly **good mark** in geometry. His parents celebrated with a special dinner. The experience taught Tuan that failure is only temporary if you are ready to try again.

passages.title: Preparing for the Big Test
passages.text:
Every **candidate** knows how stressful the week before an exam can be. Hoa is no exception. She decided to **do some revision** each morning and to **do exam preparation** in the library with a study group. She tried to **work on** her writing skills by reading model answers, and she **did an essay** every second day.

Her teacher advised her to **get through** one unit per day so that she could finish the whole course before the test. Hoa **found it difficult to** concentrate at first because her phone kept ringing, so she switched it off.

Later, when she opened her results, she saw that her **grade** was higher than she expected. Her friends were amazed, and Hoa smiled. For her, the lesson was clear: careful organisation and steady practice are more valuable than any last-minute panic.

passages.title: Luck and Hard Work
passages.text:
Last spring my cousin Nam took the national university entrance test. For months he spent every evening on **exam preparation**, studying old papers and asking teachers for help. His mother often said that success comes from **hard work**, not from luck, and Nam agreed.

In the final week, he focused on **revision** rather than learning new topics. He made small cards with key formulas and carried them on the bus. The night before the test, he went to bed early and told his family, 'With a bit of luck, I will do well.' The phrase **with a bit of luck** made everyone laugh, because he had studied so seriously.

When the results were announced, he saw that his **mark** in physics was nearly perfect. The family celebrated with a big meal, and Nam thanked everyone who had supported him. He now plans to study engineering, and he says that the long months of effort were worth every minute.
